method_card.title: Scatter Diagrams, Population Pyramids and Choropleth Maps
method_card.content:
A scatter diagram plots pairs of values (bivariate data) to show the relationship between two variables. The pattern indicates the type and strength of correlation: positive correlation (both increase together), negative correlation (one increases as the other decreases), or no correlation (no pattern). Strength is described as strong, moderate or weak depending on how closely points cluster around a straight line.

Critical rule: correlation does not imply causation. Even a very strong correlation does not mean one variable causes the other — there may be a confounding variable.

A line of best fit is drawn through the mean point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\) to minimise overall distance from points. Use it to estimate values within the data range (interpolation). Estimating outside the data range is extrapolation and is unreliable.

A population pyramid is a back-to-back horizontal bar chart showing the age-gender structure of a population. Left bars = males, right = females. Compare pyramids by commenting on shape (wide base = young/growing; wide top = ageing), relative male/female bars, and overall size.

A choropleth map uses shading to represent data values for geographic regions. Always read the key before interpreting. Students will not be asked to draw these diagrams — only to read and interpret them.
steps: Describe correlation by direction (positive/negative/none) and strength (strong/moderate/weak)
Never claim causation from correlation alone
To use a line of best fit, read up from the x-value to the line, then across to the y-axis
State whether an estimate is interpolation (within range — reliable) or extrapolation (outside — less reliable)
For population pyramids, identify the widest age group and describe the overall shape
For choropleth maps, use the key to identify the shading category and read the data range

exam_context.marks: 2–5 marks; correlation identification is 1 mark; reading from a line of best fit is 1–2 marks; population pyramid comparison is 3–4 marks
exam_context.frequency: Scatter diagrams appear on virtually every paper; population pyramid comparison and choropleth interpretation appear on roughly two-thirds of papers

worked_examples.question: The scatter diagram below shows hours of sunshine and ice cream sales. What type of correlation is shown?

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify the pattern
steps.content: As sunshine hours increase, sales also increase — both variables increase together.

steps.label: Step 2 — Name the correlation
steps.content: When both variables increase together, this is positive correlation.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Positive correlation. As hours of sunshine increase, ice cream sales tend to increase.

worked_examples.question: A line of best fit passes through (2, 14) and (8, 26). Estimate the y-value when x = 5.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: When x = 5, estimated y = 20. This is interpolation (within range 2–8), so the estimate is reliable.

worked_examples.question: Two population pyramids are shown below. Country A has wide bars at ages 0–14 and narrow bars at ages 65+. Country B has roughly equal bar widths with a bulge at 45–64. Compare the two populations in context.

steps.label: Step 1 — Describe Country A
steps.content: Country A is wide at the base (many children aged 0–14) and narrow at the top (few elderly). This is a young, rapidly growing population.

steps.label: Step 2 — Describe Country B
steps.content: Country B has a more uniform distribution with a bulge at 45–64, suggesting an ageing population with low birth rates and high life expectancy.

steps.label: Step 3 — Compare in context
steps.content: Country A has more young dependants; Country B faces greater pension and healthcare pressure. Country B needs to support an ageing population; Country A needs expanded education and employment.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Country A has a young, growing population (wide base); Country B has an ageing population. They face different demographic challenges.

bronze.display: The scatter diagram below shows car age vs value. What type of correlation is shown?
options: Positive correlation
Negative correlation
No correlation
Perfect correlation

misconceptions.message: When one variable increases and the other decreases, this is negative correlation. 'Negative' refers to the direction, not the quality of the relationship.

bronze.display: The scatter diagram below shows a clear pattern. What is the best description of the correlation?
options: Strong negative correlation
No correlation
Moderate positive correlation
Perfect positive correlation

misconceptions.message: Bottom-left to top-right = positive direction. Points not perfectly on a line = moderate strength, not perfect.

bronze.display: A choropleth map uses shading: light grey = £20,000–£30,000; medium grey = £30,000–£40,000; dark grey = £40,000–£50,000. A region shaded medium grey has income in which range?
options: Cannot tell from the map alone
bronze.display:
ShadingIncome band
░░ Light£20,000–£30,000
▒▒ Medium£30,000–£40,000
█ Dark£40,000–£50,000

A region has medium grey shading. Which income band does it fall in?

misconceptions.message: Always read the choropleth key. Medium grey is defined as £30,000–£40,000. Do not assume the darkest shade always represents the highest value — check the key.

bronze.display: The population pyramid below shows two age groups. What does the wide base (ages 0–14) suggest about the population?
options: An ageing population with low birth rates
A young, growing population with high birth rates
A stable population with equal numbers at all ages
A declining population with more elderly than young
bronze.display: What does the wide base suggest?

misconceptions.message: A wide base (ages 0–14) means many young people = high birth rate = growing population.

bronze.display: The scatter diagram below shows a line of best fit. What is the gradient of this line?

misconceptions.message: Gradient = (25 − 5) / (10 − 0) = 20/10 = 2. The line passes through (0,5) and (10,25).

bronze.display: The scatter diagram below shows TV hours vs exam scores. A student concludes 'Watching more TV causes lower exam scores.' Is this valid?
options: Yes — the pattern proves causation
No — this shows negative correlation but not causation
Yes — strong negative correlation establishes causation
No — the diagram shows positive correlation

misconceptions.message: A downward slope shows negative correlation. This does NOT prove causation — never say watching TV causes lower scores from a scatter diagram alone.

bronze.display: The population pyramid below has all male bars wider than female bars across all age groups. What does this suggest?
options: Significantly more males than females in the population
The female population is older on average
The male birth rate is lower than the female birth rate
Both populations are equal in size
bronze.display: What does this pattern suggest?

misconceptions.message: Left bars = males; right bars = females. Consistently wider left bars means more males across all age groups.

bronze.display: The scatter diagram below shows a line of best fit with equation y = 3x + 7. Estimate y when x = 4.

silver.display: The scatter diagram below shows a line of best fit passing through the mean point (5, 18) and also through (9, 30). Estimate y when x = 7.
The scatter diagram below has data in the range x = 3–10. A farmer wants to estimate yield at x = 15. Is this reliable?
options: Yes — the line can always be extended
No — x = 15 is outside the data range (3–10), making this extrapolation, which is unreliable
Yes — strong positive correlation makes extrapolation accurate
No — the equation cannot be used for predictions at all

misconceptions.message: x = 15 lies outside the observed range 3–10. This is extrapolation — less reliable because the relationship may not continue in the same way.

silver.display: The two population pyramids (simplified) show Country P and Country Q. Which country has the higher proportion of under-15s?
options: Country Q (15%)
Country P (40%)
Both countries have the same proportion
Cannot tell from the data given
silver.display:

Which country has the higher proportion of under-15s?

misconceptions.message: Country P: 18+22=40%. Country Q: 6+9=15%. Country P has a much younger population profile.

silver.display: A choropleth map shows unemployment in 4 bands (0–5%, 5–10%, 10–15%, 15%+). A journalist says 'the darkest region has unemployment exactly three times the lightest.' Is this necessarily correct?
options: Yes — the darkest band (15%+) is exactly three times the lightest band (5%)
No — the darkest region is 15%+ (could be 20%) and the lightest is 0–5% (could be 0%). Exact values cannot be compared from shading alone.
Yes — choropleth maps always show exact values
No — the lightest shading always means zero

misconceptions.message: Choropleth maps show a range, not an exact value. You cannot compare exact values from shading alone.

silver.display: The scatter diagram shows price vs units sold. The line of best fit is y = −2.5x + 120. Estimate units sold when price = 30.
A student says larger shoe size improves reading ability because there is a strong positive correlation. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Nothing — strong correlation always implies causation
Correlation does not imply causation; both increase with the child's age (confounding variable)
The correlation must be negative for reading ability
Causation can only be concluded from negative correlation

misconceptions.message: The confounding variable is age: as children get older, both feet and reading ability develop. Larger feet don't cause better reading.

gold.display: The scatter diagram shows 12 data points (x range 5–25). The mean point is (15, 42) and the line also passes through (5, 22). Which equation is correct?
The two population pyramids (summarised) show a city in 2000 and 2025. What does this suggest about the city's demographic change?
options: The population is getting younger due to increased birth rates
The population has aged over 25 years, with falling birth rates and increasing life expectancy
The city has seen a large influx of young migrants
The population size has remained constant with unchanged age structure
gold.display:
Age group2000 (% of total)2025 (% of total)
0–143014
15–444035
45–642032

What does this change suggest?

misconceptions.message: A shift from a large 0–14 group to a large 45–64 group over 25 years shows the same cohort ageing through the pyramid plus a shrinking base (fewer births). This is demographic ageing.

gold.display: The scatter diagram below shows revision hours (x range 0–12) vs exam marks. The line of best fit predicts 102 marks for 14 hours. Why is this problematic?
options: 14 hours always guarantees full marks, so 102 is an underestimate
x = 14 is outside the observed data range, making this unreliable extrapolation; also marks are capped at 100, so 102 is impossible
The correlation is only moderate so no prediction can be made
Lines of best fit cannot produce values above the mean y-value

misconceptions.message: Two problems: (1) x=14 is beyond the data range 0–12 — extrapolation is unreliable. (2) Exam marks are bounded at 100, so a predicted value of 102 is impossible.

gold.display: A choropleth map shows Region A in the highest band (75–80 years life expectancy) and Region B in the second band (70–75 years). A student claims Region A residents live 10 years longer. Is this correct?
options: Yes — the bands are 5 years apart so 10 years is correct
No — the actual difference could be as small as 0 years or as large as 10 years; shading only confirms ranges, not exact values
No — choropleth maps cannot compare two regions
Yes — darker shading always means a larger value
gold.display:
Shading bandLife expectancy
Band 4 (darkest)75–80 years
Band 370–75 years
Band 265–70 years
Band 1 (lightest)60–65 years

Region A is in Band 4. Region B is in Band 3. Is the student's claim that A lives 10 years longer correct?

misconceptions.message: If A=75.1 and B=74.9, the difference is only 0.2 years. The shading gives a range, so the actual difference is unknown without exact data.

gold.display: The scatter diagram below plots doctors per 1,000 people vs infant mortality per 1,000 births for 15 countries. A journalist writes: 'More doctors proves that increasing doctor numbers reduces infant deaths.' Evaluate this conclusion.
options: Fully supported — strong negative correlation establishes causation
Partly right — more doctors correlates with lower mortality, but overall national wealth may be a confounding variable, not a direct causal link
Wrong — negative correlation means the variables are unrelated
Correct — the journalist used the word 'proves', implying a statistical test was conducted

misconceptions.message: Strong correlation does not establish causation. Wealthier countries tend to have both more doctors AND lower infant mortality. The scatter diagram cannot separate the direct effect of doctors from the indirect effect of national wealth.

gold.display: The scatter diagram below shows the relationship between hours spent on social media and hours spent on physical exercise for 10 students. The mean point is (4, 3). A student claims 'the diagram shows that social media causes people to exercise less.' Evaluate this claim.
options: Correct — the strong negative correlation proves the causal relationship
The diagram shows negative correlation between social media use and exercise, but this does not prove causation — a third factor such as available free time could influence both
Incorrect — the correlation is positive, not negative
Correct — any scatter diagram with r close to −1 establishes causation

misconceptions.message: Even strong negative correlation does not prove causation. Available free time, lifestyle habits, or other factors could drive both variables. A scatter diagram cannot isolate the causal mechanism.
